ESR 140.13 is the default long-support channel; Release 153 is the current mainstream channel and includes newer policy controls such as AIControls and VisualSearchEnabled.
Compare the target browser fleet with the supported channels: ESR 140.13 or Release 153.
Choose ESR 140.13 when the profile is intended for the supported Extended Support Release deployment.
Choose Release 153 when the profile needs current Release-only controls, including supported AI and visual search policies.
Validate after choosing the channel and before saving, export, or handoff.
The profile uses the schema channel that matches the intended Firefox deployment.
Recovery: if validation reports unsupported, unavailable, deprecated, or unknown settings, confirm the schema channel before editing policy values.
Edit the raw policies.json document with the locally bundled Monaco editor.
Open JSON Editor for a saved profile.
The Monaco editor is bundled locally and edits the raw JSON text.
BPM still validates before saving to the normalized profile model.
Edit only the policy, preference, or raw value required by the task.
Keep the top-level policies object and valid JSON syntax.
Use validation before saving the raw edit.
The editor contains the intended raw JSON change and is ready for validation.
Recovery: if the edit becomes confusing, format the document or discard changes before saving.
Apply or edit a Firefox policy or managed preference value from the All Settings detail panel.
Open a setting detail panel for a supported editable value.
Detail editing keeps the change focused on one setting while reusing shared validation and save behavior.
Inspect the current value and validation state.
Enter or choose the new policy or managed preference value.
Apply the detail edit and watch for validation feedback.
Save the profile when the edited value is valid and intentional.
The selected policy or managed preference has the new value in the profile.
Recovery: if validation fails, correct the value shape or reset the detail before saving.
Filter configured settings by baseline, CIS, manual, imported, or raw source attribution.
Open All Settings in Configured mode or a source-aware list.
Source filters explain why a value exists.
They help distinguish generated baselines, CIS layers, manual edits, imported policies, and raw fallback values.
Choose baseline, CIS, manual, imported, or raw depending on the question you are answering.
Review the list count and visible badges after each filter change.
Clear the filter before switching to a different investigation path.
The visible list contains only settings from the selected source category.
Recovery: if a setting disappears, clear source filters and inspect its detail panel for the recorded source.
Follow focused links between search, All Settings, Guided context, and JSON locations.
A link or search result points to a setting, review state, raw key, deprecated item, or JSON location.
Deep links preserve orientation by opening the right editor and focusing the relevant setting or raw location.
Open the focused link from search, review, comparison, Guided, or JSON context.
Confirm the destination editor and focused setting or state.
Use the detail panel, filter, or JSON location to complete the task.
Return to the previous surface only after saving or discarding changes deliberately.
The linked setting opens in the correct surface with focus preserved.
Recovery: if the link cannot resolve, search by exact policy ID, preference key, or raw path.
Format the current JSON document before review, validation, or handoff.
Open JSON Editor with a JSON document in the editor.
Formatting changes whitespace and indentation only.
It should make review easier without changing the policy meaning.
Review the resulting indentation and object layout.
Confirm no policy value changed during formatting.
Validate the document after formatting if you plan to save.
The JSON document is easier to review and remains semantically unchanged.
Recovery: if formatting fails, fix JSON syntax first; trailing commas and missing braces are common causes.
Inspect imported unknown keys and raw-fallback values without losing them accidentally.
Open Review mode or a raw/unknown filtered list in All Settings.
Raw and unknown settings may come from import, schema differences, or values BPM cannot model visually.
Treat them as preservation and review items, not routine edits.
Filter or open Review items for raw, unknown, or imported settings.
Inspect the raw value, source, validation state, and schema channel.
Decide whether to preserve, remove, reset, or inspect the value in JSON Editor.
Save only after confirming the value should remain or be removed.
Raw and unknown values are preserved or removed intentionally.
Recovery: if the value might be important, export or compare the profile before removing it.
Use Configured mode to understand what the profile currently applies by domain, category, and source.
Open a saved profile in All Settings.
Configured mode focuses on values already present in the profile, not on every possible policy.
Domain summaries help you explain the active configuration.
Review the configured summary cards by domain or category.
Open a category to inspect the settings applied there.
Use source filters if you need to separate baseline, CIS, manual, imported, or raw values.
You can describe the active policy and managed preference values applied by the profile.
Recovery: if a value is missing, switch to Catalog mode or clear source filters before deciding it is absent.
Select a setting and inspect its value, source, validation, schema support, and product location.
Open All Settings and select a setting row from Review, Configured, Catalog, search, or a deep link.
The detail panel is the safe place to understand a single setting before editing it.
It shows value shape, source attribution, validation issues, and navigation context.
Select the setting row you need to understand.
Read the current value, source badge, validation messages, and schema/channel support.
Check the product location or related surface link if the setting is also covered elsewhere.
Decide whether to edit, remove, reset, or leave the value unchanged.
You understand what the setting does in this profile and what action is safe next.
Recovery: if the value shape is unclear, compare with JSON Editor or leave the setting unchanged until validation guidance is available.
Navigate All Settings categories and mapped control clusters to find related policy and preference controls.
Open All Settings in Configured or Catalog mode.
Categories group settings by product domain rather than by file location.
They help users move between browser access, privacy, search, extensions, raw/unmapped, and other clusters.
Open the category navigation or catalog summary.
Choose the domain or cluster that matches the configuration goal.
Review category counts for configured, attention, raw, or deprecated settings.
Open a setting detail or switch filters without losing the category context.
You can move through the settings inventory by product domain and reach the relevant detail panel.
Recovery: if a category does not contain the expected control, search by policy ID or inspect raw/unmapped items.
Remove a configured value or reset it back to the inherited baseline, preset, or unconfigured state.
Open the setting detail panel for a configured value.
Remove and reset actions are destructive for the selected value, so the user should understand source and downstream effects first.
Inspect the current value and source badge.
Choose Remove or Reset only for the setting you intend to change.
Read any warning or validation message shown by the detail panel.
Save the profile after confirming the value is absent, reset, or inherited as expected.
The setting no longer applies from the previous configured value.
Recovery: if the removal was unintended, reapply the previous value from history, import, comparison, or a saved source document.
Find CIS recommendations requiring manual review and decide whether to configure, document, or leave them for external verification.
Open All Settings Review mode for a profile that includes a CIS layer or CIS-derived source metadata.
Some CIS recommendations cannot be fully automated by BPM.
Review mode surfaces those items so the user can make an explicit decision without claiming certification.
Open Review mode and filter for CIS manual-review items if needed.
Read the recommendation identifiers, affected policy or preference, and current value.
Configure a supported value, document why manual verification remains, or leave the item intentionally unresolved.
Revalidate and record the decision before export or handoff.
CIS manual-review items are configured, documented, or intentionally left for external verification.
Recovery: if the recommendation cannot be mapped to a visible setting, keep the item in review and consult the CIS guide when that guide is authored.
Use Review mode to triage invalid, CIS manual-review, raw, unknown, deprecated, and imported items before routine editing.
Open a saved profile in All Settings.
Review mode is the default attention-first view.
It gathers settings that may require a decision before export, comparison, or handoff.
Open All Settings and stay in Review mode.
Read the review summary and grouped action cards.
Open each invalid, CIS manual-review, raw, unknown, deprecated, or imported item that applies to the profile.
Resolve the item, document why it remains, or move to the linked detail view for a deliberate edit.
Attention items are either resolved, intentionally retained, or ready for a focused detail edit.
Recovery: if Review looks empty but you expected issues, clear filters, refresh the profile, and confirm the selected schema channel.
Save a valid raw JSON document back to the canonical BPM profile.
The JSON document has been validated or the remaining warnings are understood.
Saving writes the raw document back through BPM normalization.
The saved profile can then be opened in Guided, All Settings, Compare, or export workflows.
Choose Save only when the top-level policies object and policy values are correct.
Wait for the saved status before leaving the route.
Reopen the profile or export policies.json when you need handoff evidence.
The BPM profile stores the JSON changes in the canonical profile model.
Recovery: if save fails, fix validation errors or return to a previous saved profile before editing again.
Search configured settings, available policies, known preferences, and setting actions from All Settings.
Search is shared across Review, Configured, and Catalog work.
It can lead to a setting, an action, or a filtered group.
Place focus in the All Settings search field.
Enter a policy ID, preference key, category, source, or plain-language term.
Choose a grouped result and confirm the target setting or action.
Clear the search when you return to browsing or filtering.
The matching setting or action is selected without losing the current profile context.
Recovery: if no result appears, confirm the schema channel and try a policy ID or preference key.
Trace a configured setting to baseline, CIS, manual, imported, or raw source attribution.
Open a configured setting in All Settings.
Source attribution helps explain why a value exists and whether changing it would override a baseline, CIS layer, manual edit, import, or raw fallback.
Open the setting detail or configured summary that shows source badges.
Identify whether the value comes from baseline, CIS, manual, imported, or raw source.
Follow related CIS or profile context links when a generated layer contributed the value.
Record the source before editing, removing, or resetting the setting.
You know where the configured value came from and can explain the impact of changing it.
Recovery: if source attribution is ambiguous, compare the profile with a clean baseline or inspect the imported source document.
Open All Settings for a saved profile when you need complete visual control beyond the shorter Guided workflow.
New unsaved drafts must be saved before All Settings can open.
All Settings is the complete visual editor for Firefox policies and known managed preferences.
It opens in Review mode so attention items are visible before broad catalog browsing.
Open the saved profile from the Library.
Choose the All Settings editor surface.
Confirm that Review, Configured, and Catalog modes are available.
Use the mode that matches the task: Review for attention, Configured for applied values, or Catalog for every supported setting.
The saved profile is open in All Settings with the correct mode available.
Recovery: if All Settings is unavailable, save the Guided draft first or reopen a saved profile from the Library.
Open the complete profile as a Firefox policies.json document for exact review or raw editing.
JSON Editor works on a saved profile and represents the profile as a Firefox boundary document.
JSON Editor is the raw document surface.
Use it when Guided or All Settings is too high-level for exact review, migration checks, troubleshooting, or raw values.
Open the saved profile from the Library or another editor.
Confirm the editor shows a top-level policies object and the download action is available.
Use JSON Editor only when exact raw document control is needed.
The current profile is visible as editable Firefox policies.json content.
Recovery: if the route cannot open, save the profile first or return to All Settings for visual editing.
Validate raw JSON syntax and Firefox policy values before saving.
Open JSON Editor with the document you want to check.
Validation distinguishes malformed JSON from policy or schema errors.
A document can parse as JSON and still fail policy validation.
If validation reports malformed JSON, fix syntax such as trailing commas or missing braces.
If validation reports policy errors, correct unsupported keys, wrong value types, or schema-channel mismatches.
Validate again until the status explains that the document is acceptable or the remaining issue is intentional for raw review.
The document has a known validation state before save or export.
Recovery: if errors are hard to read, use All Settings to inspect the affected policy or preference visually.

fragments: Use the current liveness and readiness probes as a lightweight operational handshake before API workflows.
For host setup, service start, logs, updates from source, and operating-system details, use the source-deployment Administrator Guide; this API topic only documents the integration handshake.
This task covers API-HEALTH-001 and API-HEALTH-002.
BPM 0.9.0 exposes prefix-free probes at /health and /health/ready.
BPM does not expose dependency diagnostics through these probes; they are not versioned and do not replace product-specific retry or incident policy.
Call the liveness probe before starting a short API sequence.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/health.
Error example: no application error is currently declared; transport, gateway, or process failures are handled outside BPM.
Call the readiness probe before operations that depend on application startup being complete.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/health/ready.
Response example: 200 {"status":"ready","ready":true}.
Error example: no degraded-state or dependency-detail body is currently exposed.
Use readiness as a gate, not as a complete dependency inventory.
When ready is true, the integrating product may continue with discovery, validation, import, export, or profile lifecycle calls.
It must not infer database health details, schema cache details, documentation portal status, queue state, or deployment topology from this response.
Keep polling and retry decisions in the integrating product.
BPM does not declare a polling interval, retry-after header, service-level objective, circuit-breaker contract, request ID, or webhook for probe changes.
Store your own timestamp, observed status, timeout, and retry decision.
Separate API handshake checks from source deployment troubleshooting.

If probes are unreachable or the response differs from the examples, switch to the source-deployment Administrator Guide for process, environment, database, log, and update-from-source checks instead of expanding this API integration task into deployment instructions.
Record the operational handshake result with the downstream API action.
A successful health or readiness response does not authenticate callers, authorize operations, reserve profile revisions, guarantee later API success, or prove Firefox runtime enforcement.
Treat it as one small preflight signal.
The integrating product has a minimal and current BPM operational handshake for liveness and readiness without depending on undocumented deployment behavior.
After a successful readiness check, continue with OpenAPI discovery or the specific API workflow topic for validation, import/export, or profile lifecycle operations.
Render one BPM profile as the Firefox Enterprise deployment document with optional download and pretty-print parameters.
Store the BPM profile ID returned by create or import.
If the profile is archived, decide explicitly whether the integration is allowed to export it with include_deleted=true.
Export reads BPM's normalized flags and returns canonical Firefox JSON with a top-level policies object.
BPM profile metadata and opaque compliance metadata are not exported into the Firefox deployment document.
Export the active profile as canonical Firefox JSON.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/export/profiles/42/firefox/policies.json.
Response example: 200 application/json with JSON {"policies":{"DisableTelemetry":true,"BlockAboutConfig":true}}.
Add download mode when the caller needs an attachment filename.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/export/profiles/42/firefox/policies.json?download=1.
Response example: 200 application/json plus Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="profile-42-policies.json".
The JSON body is the same deployment document.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/export/profiles/42/firefox/policies.json?pretty=1 selects indentation of two spaces when indent is omitted.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/export/profiles/42/firefox/policies.json?indent=0 uses the explicit indentation parameter.
Error example: 422 for invalid constrained query values.
Export an archived profile only when the external workflow has a review reason.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/export/profiles/42/firefox/policies.json?include_deleted=true&download=1&pretty=1.
Error examples: 404 when a missing or archived profile is not visible; 422 for invalid path or query input.
Validate the exported document before handing it to another system.
Request example: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/validate/release-153 with JSON {"document":{"policies":{"DisableTelemetry":true,"BlockAboutConfig":true}}}.
Response example: 200 {"ok":true,"profile":"release-153"}.
Validation confirms schema shape, not Firefox runtime deployment success.
Record the exact exported artifact externally.
Export has no ETag, precondition header, bulk endpoint, or transaction wrapper.
Record the profile ID, revision observed before export, schema channel, query parameters, exported document hash, and downstream handoff decision outside BPM.
The integration has a canonical Firefox policies.json artifact that excludes BPM-only metadata and can be supplied to deployment tooling.
If validation fails or the profile revision changed between read and export, stop the handoff and refresh the profile state.
Create a normalized BPM profile from a canonical Firefox Enterprise policies.json document using JSON or multipart input.
Set $BPM_BASE_URL, choose a supported schema channel such as release-153, and prepare a full Firefox document with a top-level policies object.
Import accepts application/json with FirefoxPoliciesJsonImportRequest or multipart/form-data with a file field.
BPM validates the canonical Firefox document, normalizes policies into profile flags, and stores optional opaque compliance metadata on the BPM profile.
Submit a JSON import request when the integrating product already has the document in memory.

Request example: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/import/firefox/policies.json with Content-Type: application/json and JSON {"name":"api-json-import","description":"Imported by control product","schema_version":"release-153","compliance":{"framework":"cis","layer":"cis_l1"},"document":{"policies":{"DisableTelemetry":true,"BlockAboutConfig":true}}}.
Use multipart import when the source system hands over a file.

Request example: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/import/firefox/policies.json with multipart/form-data, fields name=api-multipart-import, schema_version=release-153, optional description, optional compliance={"framework":"cis","layer":"cis_l2"} as a JSON string, and file=@policies.json;type=application/json.
Runtime also accepts a multipart document field, but the OpenAPI multipart schema currently declares file; use file for new examples.
Read the created BPM profile from the 201 ProfileRead response.
Response example: 201 ProfileRead with schema_version="release-153", flags.DisableTelemetry=true, flags.BlockAboutConfig=true, stored compliance, id, and revision.
Store the returned profile ID instead of inferring identity from the profile name.
Treat import errors as profile creation failures and do not assume partial profile state.

Error examples: 400 for malformed JSON, wrong document shape, or unsupported schema channel; 409 for duplicate profile name; 415 for unsupported media type; 422 for request or Firefox policy validation errors.
Keep canonical Firefox and normalized BPM shapes separate in integration code.
The request document.policies is the Firefox deployment boundary.
The created profile's flags are BPM's normalized model.
Do not send a top-level flags object to this import endpoint.
Record import evidence in the integrating product.
Import creates a BPM profile but does not deploy Firefox settings, prove runtime enforcement, or provide an idempotency key.
Record the source document hash, schema channel, returned profile ID, revision, compliance metadata, and duplicate-name recovery decision externally.
The Firefox policies.json document is represented as a normalized BPM profile that can be reviewed, validated, exported, and tracked by ID.
Use the export task to render the saved profile back to canonical Firefox JSON before handing it to deployment tooling.
Use destructive profile lifecycle endpoints with explicit review and recovery records.
Confirm the target profile ID, current lifecycle state, and external approval record before calling destructive endpoints.
This task covers API-PROFILE-006, API-PROFILE-007, API-PROFILE-008, and API-PROFILE-009.
BPM 0.9.0 has no bulk confirmation token, no undo endpoint for permanent delete, and no transaction rollback across operations.
Archive a profile when you need to remove it from active workflows while preserving it for review.
Archive is a destructive lifecycle change for active workflows.
Record the approval reason and profile ID before the call.
Request example: DELETE $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/42.
Response example: 204 with no JSON body.
Error examples: 404 missing profile or 422 invalid path input.
Restore an archived profile only after checking whether the name and profile purpose are still valid.
Request example: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/42/restore.
Error examples: 404 profile cannot be restored or found; 422 invalid path input.
Permanently delete a profile only when the external retention policy allows removal.
Permanent delete removes an active or archived profile and has no BPM undo endpoint.
Export or record required evidence before the call.
Request example: DELETE $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/42/hard.
Reset the profile library only in disposable or explicitly approved environments.
Reset permanently deletes every profile in the Library and currently requires no confirmation token.
Never use it as a routine synchronization shortcut.
Request example: DELETE $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/reset.
Error behavior: no application error is currently declared; database failures use framework handling.
After any destructive call, re-list profiles and read the affected record when applicable.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles?lifecycle=all.
Use this verification to update the integrating product's inventory state.
Write the external audit record with operation ID, HTTP method, path, profile ID, approver, reason, timestamp, response status, and recovery decision.
Expected result: a later reviewer can distinguish archive, restore, hard delete, and reset actions and can see why the integration considered the operation safe.
Destructive profile lifecycle operations are documented with request, response, error, warning, and recovery evidence.
If the approval record is missing, stop the integration workflow before calling permanent delete or reset.
Rolling upgrades are planned but not implemented yet.
Use existing health, import, validation, profile, and export APIs to hand off a reviewed Firefox document with compliance evidence.
Set $BPM_BASE_URL, choose the schema channel, and decide which system owns the source document, compliance scan result, reviewer approval, exported artifact, and recovery decision.
This scenario uses API-HEALTH-001, API-HEALTH-002, API-FF-001, API-PROFILE-003, API-VAL-001, and API-FF-002.
BPM stores the normalized profile and opaque compliance metadata; the integrating product owns scan interpretation and downstream deployment.
Start with health and readiness before the handoff sequence.
Request examples: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/health and GET $BPM_BASE_URL/health/ready.
Response examples: 200 {"status":"ok"} and 200 {"status":"ready","ready":true}.
Error example: transport or gateway failure is handled outside BPM because no application error is currently declared.
Import the reviewed Firefox document with compliance metadata attached to the BPM profile.

Request example: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/import/firefox/policies.json with JSON {"name":"reviewed-corp-baseline","schema_version":"release-153","compliance":{"scanner":"external-control","result":"passed","ticket":"SEC-42"},"document":{"policies":{"DisableTelemetry":true,"BlockAboutConfig":true}}}.
Read the created profile and record BPM ownership fields separately from external evidence.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/42.
Response example: 200 ProfileRead with id, revision, flags, schema_version, and opaque compliance.
Validate the canonical Firefox document that will be handed off.
Request example: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/validate/release-153 with JSON {"document":{"policies":{"DisableTelemetry":true,"BlockAboutConfig":true}}}.
Response example: 200 {"ok":true,"profile":"release-153"}.
Export the BPM profile as the canonical Firefox deployment document.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/export/profiles/42/firefox/policies.json?download=1&pretty=1.
Response example: 200 application/json with Content-Disposition and top-level policies.
BPM profile metadata and compliance metadata are not exported.
Stop on mismatches and write the failure recovery record.
If import, validation, read-back, or export evidence differs from the approved source document, do not retry blindly.
Store source hash, profile ID, revision, validation body, export hash, scanner result, reviewer, response status, and the recovery decision outside BPM.
The integrating product has an executable import-review-export flow with compliance handoff, canonical export, and explicit recovery evidence.
Use deployment tooling outside BPM to apply the exported policies.json; BPM validation does not prove Firefox runtime enforcement.
Use existing profile and validation APIs to pull BPM state, compare it externally, and update one profile with explicit ownership and concurrency evidence.
Set $BPM_BASE_URL and decide which external control product owns comparison logic, desired-state calculation, retry policy, and audit records.
BPM does not expose a compare API or transaction wrapper.
This scenario uses API-PROFILE-001, API-PROFILE-003, API-PROFILE-005, and API-VAL-001.
BPM owns stored profile state and validation.
The integrating product owns desired state, comparison output, reviewer approval, and retry decisions.
Pull candidate profiles from the Library with the same filter rules the control product uses for ownership.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles?q=corp&lifecycle=active&limit=50&offset=0.
Error example: 422 for invalid query input.
Read each selected profile by ID and store its current revision.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/42.
Response example: 200 ProfileRead with flags, compliance, schema_version, and revision.
Error examples: 404 missing or archived profile; 422 invalid path input.
Compare the pulled profile with external desired state outside BPM.
Expected result: the integrating product records changed policy keys, unchanged keys, missing keys, reviewer, and source of desired state.
Do not assume a BPM compare endpoint, marketplace connector, or certified workflow exists.
Validate the candidate Firefox document before applying the update.
Request example: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/validate/release-153 with JSON {"document":{"policies":{"DisableTelemetry":true,"BlockAboutConfig":true}}}.
Response example: 200 {"ok":true,"profile":"release-153"}.
Error examples: 400, 404, 422, or 503 depending on document shape, channel, policy validity, and schema availability.
Patch the BPM profile only with the revision observed before comparison.

Request example: PATCH $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/42 with JSON {"flags":{"DisableTelemetry":true,"BlockAboutConfig":true},"expected_revision":7,"compliance":{"source":"control-product","decision":"approved"}}.
Response example: 200 ProfileRead with incremented revision.
Error examples: 400, 404, 409 stale expected_revision, or 422.
If validation fails, the revision is stale, or the update result does not match the intended desired state, stop the workflow, re-read BPM state, and create an external audit record.
BPM does not provide a multi-operation transaction, automatic rollback, idempotency key, or safe retry contract.
The control product has an executable pull/compare/update flow with explicit state ownership, validation evidence, revision protection, and failure recovery boundaries.
If the updated profile must be deployed elsewhere, continue with the Firefox export task and preserve the profile ID, revision, validation response, and approval record.
Use profile list, stats, read, create, and update endpoints without assuming bulk or transactional behavior.
Set $BPM_BASE_URL and read /openapi.json for the current ProfileCreate, ProfileUpdate, and ProfileRead shapes.
This task covers API-PROFILE-001, API-PROFILE-002, API-PROFILE-003, API-PROFILE-004, and API-PROFILE-005.
Store returned id and revision; do not infer identity from name alone.
List profiles with filters before choosing a profile to synchronize.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles?q=corp&lifecycle=active&limit=50&offset=0&sort=updated_at&order=desc.
Error example: 422 for invalid typed or ranged query input.
Read profile statistics for the same filter context when you need counts.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/stats?q=corp&lifecycle=active.
Error example: 422 for invalid query input.
Read the selected profile by integer ID and include archived records only when required.
Request example: GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/42?include_deleted=false.
Response example: 200 ProfileRead with id, revision, timestamps, lifecycle, and validation state.
Error example: 404 for a missing or not-visible profile; 422 for invalid path or query input.
Create a normalized BPM profile only when the integration owns the new profile name.
Request example: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles with JSON {"name":"corp-baseline","schema_version":"firefox-152","flags":{},"compliance":{}}.
Error examples: 400 invalid schema/profile, 409 duplicate name, or 422 request or policy validation.
Update mutable fields with PATCH and send expected_revision when you need optimistic concurrency.
Request example: PATCH $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/42 with JSON {"description":"Reviewed by control plane","expected_revision":7}.
Response example: 200 ProfileRead with incremented revision after a material update.
Error examples: 400 invalid schema/profile, 404 missing or archived profile, 409 stale expected_revision, or 422 validation error.
Record the synchronized profile ID, revision, validation state, schema channel, and any opaque compliance metadata in the integrating product.
BPM does not provide a multi-operation transaction.
If a later step fails, the integrating product owns recovery, audit records, and retry decisions.
The integration has a reproducible profile synchronization path for list, stats, read, create, and update operations.
Use the destructive lifecycle task before archive, restore, permanent delete, or reset operations.
Request example: export BPM_BASE_URL="${BPM_BASE_URL:?set BPM_BASE_URL first}".
Request example: session.post(f"{base_url}/api/validate/{schema_channel}", json=payload, timeout=10).
Use the validation endpoint as a preflight gate for candidate Firefox Enterprise policies.json documents and structured error handling.
Choose the target schema channel, such as release-153 or esr-140.13, and prepare a ValidationRequest body with a full Firefox document in document.policies.
BPM validates candidate policies.json content before import, export handoff, or an external policy-review gate.
A plain policy mapping is still accepted for compatibility, but new integration examples use the full Firefox policies.json shape.
Submit a successful validation request for the selected schema channel.
Request example: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/validate/release-153 with JSON {"document":{"policies":{"DisableTelemetry":true,"BlockAboutConfig":true}}}.
Response example: 200 {"ok":true,"profile":"release-153"}.
Treat ok=false as a failed gate even when HTTP status is 200.
Request example: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/validate/release-153 with JSON {"document":123}.
Response example: 200 {"ok":false,"profile":"release-153","detail":"Expected object with policy mappings","error":"Expected object with policy mappings"}.
Check the response body, not HTTP status alone.
Handle malformed canonical Firefox document errors as request-shape failures.
Request example: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/validate/release-153 with JSON {"document":{"policies":[]}}.
Error example: 400 with detail.message="Firefox policies.json validation failed" and detail.issues[].path pointing to policies.
Reject unsupported schema channels before trusting validation results.
Request example: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/validate/beta-999 with JSON {"document":{"policies":{"DisableTelemetry":true}}}.
Error example: 404 with detail text Unknown profile 'beta-999'.
A registered but unavailable schema returns 503.
Map policy validation failures to actionable reviewer feedback.
Request example: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/validate/release-153 with JSON {"document":{"policies":{"Proxy":{"Mode":"bogus"}}}}.
Error example: 422 with detail.message="Policy validation failed" and issue fields policy, path, and message.
Record the validation decision in the integrating product.
Validation is a schema and policy-shape gate only.
It does not deploy Firefox, prove runtime enforcement, authenticate callers, reserve a profile revision, or provide an idempotency key.
Store the channel, candidate document hash, response status, ok value, structured issues, and reviewer decision externally.
The integration can block unsafe candidate policies.json handoffs and preserve structured evidence for success and failure decisions.
If validation succeeds, continue to import, profile update, or export handoff using the same schema channel and recorded candidate hash.
Diagnose local SQLite, storage path, backup, and profile visibility issues without editing database rows directly.
Use this procedure when profiles disappear, writes fail, migration evidence is unclear, backup checksums do not match, or BPM_DATABASE_URL points to an unexpected location.
Current source deployment uses local storage such as sqlite+aiosqlite:///./data/bpm.db and repository-owned files under data/, schema cache paths, and documentation site paths.
There is no managed backup or restore orchestration in BPM 0.9.0.
Confirm the active database URL and working directory.
Record BPM_DATABASE_URL, current directory, source revision, and whether the process runs from Linux filesystem or /mnt/c.
Do not assume two shells point at the same data/bpm.db.
Check migration and profile API evidence before opening storage files.
Focused rerun: alembic upgrade head, then curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/profiles?limit=50.
If the API returns expected profiles, the symptom may be filter, lifecycle, or browser state.
Verify backup evidence before destructive recovery.
Check mkdir -p backups, cp data/bpm.db backups/bpm-pre-update.db, and sha256sum backups/bpm-pre-update.db records.
Keep exports of critical policies.json profiles as separate evidence.
Do not edit SQLite rows, generated artifacts, or schema cache files as routine recovery.
Use documented profile archive, restore, import, export, or update-from-source procedures instead.
Escalate with storage evidence when recovery is unsafe.
Include database URL, file path, checksum, migration command, API response, and backup/export evidence.
If no verified pre-failure backup exists, stop before deleting or replacing data/bpm.db; BPM does not provide point-in-time recovery.
The operator has a storage diagnosis that preserves user data and separates database state from UI or filter symptoms.
After storage is stable, rerun health/readiness and the smallest affected API workflow.
Troubleshoot documentation portal build and link failures
Diagnose /help/ build, manifest, search, source-link, and generated-link failures without patching built artifacts.
Use this procedure when make docs-validate, make docs-build, make test-docs-contract, /help/, or generated documentation links fail during source operation or update-from-source checks.
Documentation portal troubleshooting belongs to source DITA, maps, keys, config, tools, and focused tests.
Built output under documentation/build/, reports, manifests, search indexes, and packages are regenerated evidence, not hand-edited source.
Start with the smallest documentation command named by the failure.
For one changed topic, run make docs-fast-check DOCS_CHANGED="documentation/src/dita/en/admin/example.dita".
For contracts, run the named documentation/tests/contract/...
For full link validation, run make docs-validate.
Classify source-link versus generated-link failures.
Source failures usually name a DITA topic, key, or fragment.
Generated-link failures appear after DITA publish and can involve manifest, target map, search, or normalized output path.
Preserve the failing path and target URL.
Fix source, map, key, config, or generator input only.
Do not patch documentation/build/, documentation/dist/, documentation/reports/, generated search indexes, or packaged artifacts by hand.
Update the DITA topic, map, keydef, config, or build tool, then rebuild.
If the static build passes but BPM /help/ reports missing, stale, incompatible, incomplete, or not-found states, check installed artifact path and manifest digest.
Preserve FastAPI /docs and /openapi.json separately.
Record the focused rerun and remaining gates.
Use make test-docs-contract, make docs-validate, and make docs-build for this troubleshooting slice.
Browser-backed docs checks, screenshots, manual QA, package verification, and product release tests remain separate gates unless explicitly run.
The operator can diagnose documentation portal failures from source and regenerate output without hand-editing disposable artifacts.
After the portal build passes, rerun the update-from-source verification topic and any affected contextual help route checks.
Troubleshoot failed startup and unreachable probes
Diagnose a source-run BPM process that does not start or does not answer health and readiness probes.
Use this procedure when make dev, uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000, GET /health, or GET /health/ready fails during source deployment or integration startup.
This diagnostic keeps process, environment, and probe evidence separate.
It does not create a systemd unit, Windows service, reverse proxy, TLS endpoint, or production restart policy.
Capture the failing command and foreground log.
Run or copy the exact command, then record stdout and stderr from the foreground terminal.
Include make dev, uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000, Python traceback summary, working directory, and source revision from git rev-parse --short HEAD.
Verify the configured host and port before changing code.
Check BPM_HOST, BPM_PORT, BPM_RELOAD, BPM_DATABASE_URL, and BPM_DOCUMENTATION_SITE_DIR.
Focused rerun: curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8000/health and curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8000/health/ready.
Separate process startup from probe reachability.
If the process is not running, fix dependency, environment, or migration evidence first.
If the process is running but probes are unreachable, check local firewall, bind address, WSL port forwarding, and whether the request targets 127.0.0.1, 0.0.0.0, or a Windows host route.
Preserve user data while collecting evidence.
Copy logs, environment names, and probe responses only.
Do not edit generated artifacts, database rows, schema cache files, or source code as routine recovery.
Do not delete data/bpm.db to make startup pass.
Choose the smallest rerun and escalation path.
Focused rerun: make test-fast for product smoke, make docs-validate only if documentation output is involved, and make test-docs-contract only for documentation contracts.
If probes remain unreachable after configuration and process checks, stop automated integration runs and escalate with command, logs, config names, and probe evidence.
The operator can distinguish a failed process, an unreachable probe, and a deployment boundary without mutating user data.
After probes pass, return to the health-gated startup or reusable API examples topic before running mutating integrations.
Troubleshoot Firefox import and export failures
Diagnose JSON import, multipart import, and Firefox policies export failures while preserving source and exported evidence.
Use this procedure when POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/import/firefox/policies.json or GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/export/profiles/42/firefox/policies.json returns 400, 404, 409, 415, or 422.

Import/export troubleshooting separates source document validity, multipart field shape, duplicate profile names, archived profile access, and canonical Firefox export from downstream deployment tooling.
Identify the operation and content type.
Record whether the request was JSON FirefoxPoliciesJsonImportRequest, multipart/form-data with file=@policies.json, or export with download=1, pretty=1, or include_deleted=true.
Validate the source Firefox document before retrying import.
Focused rerun: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/validate/release-153 with the same document.policies.
If validation fails, fix the source document outside BPM before another import.
For 409, choose a new synthetic profile name or archive/restore intentionally.
For 415, verify application/json or multipart upload fields.
For 422, record field-level errors and do not rewrite profile storage directly.
For 404, re-read GET $BPM_BASE_URL/api/profiles/42?include_deleted=true.
For archived profiles, decide whether include_deleted=true is appropriate.
Compare exported document hash with the reviewed source hash; BPM profile metadata and compliance metadata are not exported.
Focused rerun: ./.venv/bin/pytest -q -m docs_contract documentation/tests/contract/test_api_integration_topics.py for documented examples.
Do not retry blindly after mismatched import/export evidence; store source hash, export hash, profile ID, revision, HTTP status, and operator decision.
The operator can identify whether the failure belongs to source JSON, multipart fields, profile lifecycle state, or export evidence.
After recovery, attach the evidence to the external control-product audit record.
Troubleshoot schema cache and API validation errors
Diagnose unavailable schema cache, unknown schema channel, and Firefox policies validation failures without patching generated schema artifacts.

Use this procedure when POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/validate/release-153, POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/validate/beta-999, or user-facing validation returns 400, 404, 422, or 503; a non-object document can return 200 ok=false with Expected object with policy mappings.
BPM validation depends on maintained schema channels and local schema/cache configuration.
The diagnostic records whether the issue is request shape, unknown profile, invalid Firefox policy data, or unavailable schema cache.
Record the exact validation request and response.
Store sanitized request body hash, schema channel, HTTP status, detail, message, error, and issues.
Keep the candidate policies.json outside logs if it contains customer values.
A non-object document or missing document.policies is operator input, not a schema-cache defect; current BPM can report this as 200 ok=false.
Focused rerun: POST $BPM_BASE_URL/api/validate/release-153 with {"document":{"policies":{"DisableTelemetry":true}}}.
Classify schema-channel and cache failures.
A profile such as beta-999 can return 404; an unavailable registered schema can return 503.
Check BPM_SCHEMA_BASE_URL, BPM_SCHEMA_CACHE_DIR, and BPM_SCHEMA_HTTP_TIMEOUT before any broader rebuild.
Use maintained refresh and validation checks.
Focused rerun: ./.venv/bin/pytest -q -m docs_contract documentation/tests/contract/test_api_openapi_drift.py for API documentation drift, or product schema tests when the API behavior changed.
Do not hand-edit app/schemas/cache or generated Firefox skeletons.
Stop unsafe recovery and preserve evidence.
If the same valid request changes status across runs, preserve response bodies, source revision, cache path, and environment variables.
Do not edit generated schema artifacts or database rows as routine recovery; separate product defects from operator payload errors.
The operator has a classified validation failure with a smallest rerun and no hidden schema mutation.
After validation succeeds, return to validate-before-apply or import-review-export workflows.
Troubleshoot WSL networking and stale dependencies
Diagnose Windows 10/11 through WSL access problems, Linux filesystem placement, and stale Python dependencies after source changes.

Use this procedure when Windows cannot reach a WSL-hosted BPM process, probes work inside WSL but not from Windows, file performance is unstable under /mnt/c, or dependencies appear stale after git checkout <approved-new-ref>.
WSL troubleshooting keeps Windows browser access, Linux process binding, filesystem placement, and Python environment refresh separate.
BPM does not provide a native Windows service or installer in 0.9.0.
Confirm where the source checkout and virtual environment live.
Prefer the Linux filesystem for the checkout and .venv.
Record whether files are under /mnt/c, which can change performance and permissions.
Do not mix multiple checkouts during diagnosis.
Verify the WSL process binding and Windows route.
Check BPM_HOST="0.0.0.0", BPM_PORT="8000", curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8000/health inside WSL, and browser access from Windows.
If Windows fails, record firewall and port-forwarding evidence.
Refresh dependencies after source movement or revision changes.
Focused rerun: source .venv/bin/activate, python -m pip install --upgrade pip, and pip install -e ".[dev]".
If dependency errors persist, record package names and source revision rather than editing installed packages manually.
Separate stale dependency symptoms from schema or database problems.
If import/export or validation fails after dependency refresh, use schema/cache and import/export troubleshooting.
If profile visibility changes, use database/storage troubleshooting.
Do not create undocumented Windows services, move the database between filesystems, or claim native installer behavior.
If WSL networking remains ambiguous, stop external integrations and escalate with WSL distro, checkout path, bind address, Windows URL, and probe outputs.
The operator can distinguish WSL routing, filesystem placement, and dependency-refresh defects without changing product storage.
After WSL access is stable, return to source deployment verification and health-gated startup.
The Firefox schema channel controls which policies and values BPM can validate and show as supported.
Choose Firefox ESR 140.13 for the supported Extended Support Release channel, or Firefox Release 153 for the current mainstream channel.
Schema choice changes available controls, validation messages, and whether a setting is supported, unavailable, deprecated, unknown, imported, or preserved as raw data.
The supported schema channels are ESR 140.13 and Release 153.
Choose the channel that matches the browser fleet before import, validation, detailed editing, or export.
Validation checks the profile against the selected schema and BPM normalized model.
Run validation before export, after JSON edits, after import, and before comparing important profiles.
Common policies such as DisableTelemetry validate in both supported channels.
Release 153 can also support newer controls such as AIControls and VisualSearchEnabled that are absent in ESR 140.13.
Supported, unavailable, deprecated, unknown, and raw states
Supported settings can be edited and validated for the selected schema.

Unavailable or unknown settings should be reviewed before handoff; deprecated settings may still exist but require current-channel confirmation; raw fallback values should be preserved or removed deliberately.
Switching schema channels is a review decision, not a silent migration.
Revalidate after switching and inspect Release-only, ESR-absent, imported, raw, or deprecated values before saving or exporting.
A common valid example uses DisableTelemetry.
A Release-only valid example can use AIControls or VisualSearchEnabled.
The same AIControls document is unsupported on ESR 140.13, and wrong value types such as a string value for DisableTelemetry are schema-invalid.
If validation fails, read the affected policy path, confirm the schema channel, inspect the setting in All Settings or JSON Editor, and only then edit, remove, or preserve the value.
Use JSON Editor for exact raw review, migration checks, troubleshooting, and values that are easier to handle as raw policies.json.
JSON Editor is powerful but less guided than the visual editors.
It should be a deliberate choice when the user needs boundary-document precision.
Use JSON Editor for exact policies.json review, migration checks, raw fallback values, or troubleshooting malformed import/export documents.
Use Guided Editor for common workflows and All Settings for full visual inspection before choosing raw JSON for routine edits.
BPM also validates Firefox policy values, schema channel support, and the canonical normalized model before save.
A valid example keeps a top-level policies object with entries such as DisableTelemetry and Preferences, including a locked browser.startup.homepage value.
Invalid examples include malformed JSON syntax and schema-invalid policy values such as a string where a boolean is required.
Use this reference to interpret clean, invalid, CIS manual-review, raw, unknown, deprecated, and imported review states.
Review states explain why All Settings asks for attention before the user edits routine values.
A clean profile has no remaining Review items.
It can still contain configured settings; it simply has no attention states that BPM can detect.
Invalid items have values that fail current validation for the selected schema channel and should be fixed or removed before handoff.
CIS manual-review items need a human decision or external verification.
BPM can surface the item without claiming certified compliance.
Raw fallback, unknown, and imported items should be preserved or removed deliberately because BPM may not be able to model their intent visually.
Deprecated settings may still exist in a profile, but the user should confirm current Release/ESR support before relying on them.
If a state is unexpected, clear filters, confirm the schema channel, refresh the profile, and inspect the setting detail before editing.
Use bounded-list behavior, search, filters, and categories when All Settings contains a large policy and preference inventory.
All Settings can expose many schema-backed policies and known preferences.
Bounded lists keep the interface usable and make the next narrowing action explicit.
All Settings may show a bounded subset, count, or continuation action instead of rendering every row at once.
Search, category navigation, source filters, and state filters are the supported ways to reduce a large inventory.
Large-inventory handling is a UI boundary, not a signal that settings are missing from the profile or catalog.
If the expected row is not visible, search by exact ID, clear filters, or switch between Configured and Catalog mode.
Add a known managed preference that is not yet configured in the profile.
Open All Settings with the correct schema channel selected.
Managed preferences complement Firefox policies when BPM exposes a known preference key and lock behavior.
Add them deliberately and validate the result.
Open the add preference control or find the preference in Catalog mode.
Choose the known preference key and review its expected value type.
Enter the value and lock state required by the profile.
Apply, validate, and save the managed preference.
The profile contains the new managed preference with the intended value and lock behavior.
Recovery: if the preference key is unknown or validation fails, remove the draft value and use JSON only for deliberate raw review.
Use Catalog mode to browse every supported policy and known managed preference for the selected schema.
Open a saved profile in All Settings.
Catalog mode is the full visual inventory.
It includes configured and available settings while keeping advanced controls behind deliberate disclosures.
Browse categories for supported policies and known managed preferences.
Use category cards or search to narrow the inventory.
Select a setting before applying, editing, or resetting a value.
You can find supported policies and known preferences without using raw JSON first.
Recovery: if the catalog is large, use search, filters, or bounded-list controls instead of scrolling blindly.
Choose between Firefox ESR 140.13 and Firefox Release 153 before importing, validating, or editing a profile.
Start this task before creating a profile, importing policies.json, or validating a raw JSON document.
The schema channel decides which Firefox policies BPM can validate and which controls are shown as supported.
ESR 140.13 is the default long-support channel; Release 153 is the current mainstream channel and includes newer policy controls such as AIControls and VisualSearchEnabled.
Compare the target browser fleet with the supported channels: ESR 140.13 or Release 153.
Choose ESR 140.13 when the profile is intended for the supported Extended Support Release deployment.
Choose Release 153 when the profile needs current Release-only controls, including supported AI and visual search policies.
Validate after choosing the channel and before saving, export, or handoff.
The profile uses the schema channel that matches the intended Firefox deployment.
Recovery: if validation reports unsupported, unavailable, deprecated, or unknown settings, confirm the schema channel before editing policy values.
Edit the raw policies.json document with the locally bundled Monaco editor.
Open JSON Editor for a saved profile.
The Monaco editor is bundled locally and edits the raw JSON text.
BPM still validates before saving to the normalized profile model.
Edit only the policy, preference, or raw value required by the task.
Keep the top-level policies object and valid JSON syntax.
Use validation before saving the raw edit.
The editor contains the intended raw JSON change and is ready for validation.
Recovery: if the edit becomes confusing, format the document or discard changes before saving.
Apply or edit a Firefox policy or managed preference value from the All Settings detail panel.
Open a setting detail panel for a supported editable value.
Detail editing keeps the change focused on one setting while reusing shared validation and save behavior.
Inspect the current value and validation state.
Enter or choose the new policy or managed preference value.
Apply the detail edit and watch for validation feedback.
Save the profile when the edited value is valid and intentional.
The selected policy or managed preference has the new value in the profile.
Recovery: if validation fails, correct the value shape or reset the detail before saving.
Filter configured settings by baseline, CIS, manual, imported, or raw source attribution.
Open All Settings in Configured mode or a source-aware list.
Source filters explain why a value exists.
They help distinguish generated baselines, CIS layers, manual edits, imported policies, and raw fallback values.
Choose baseline, CIS, manual, imported, or raw depending on the question you are answering.
Review the list count and visible badges after each filter change.
Clear the filter before switching to a different investigation path.
The visible list contains only settings from the selected source category.
Recovery: if a setting disappears, clear source filters and inspect its detail panel for the recorded source.
Follow focused links between search, All Settings, Guided context, and JSON locations.
A link or search result points to a setting, review state, raw key, deprecated item, or JSON location.
Deep links preserve orientation by opening the right editor and focusing the relevant setting or raw location.
Open the focused link from search, review, comparison, Guided, or JSON context.
Confirm the destination editor and focused setting or state.
Use the detail panel, filter, or JSON location to complete the task.
Return to the previous surface only after saving or discarding changes deliberately.
The linked setting opens in the correct surface with focus preserved.
Recovery: if the link cannot resolve, search by exact policy ID, preference key, or raw path.
Format the current JSON document before review, validation, or handoff.
Open JSON Editor with a JSON document in the editor.
Formatting changes whitespace and indentation only.
It should make review easier without changing the policy meaning.
Review the resulting indentation and object layout.
Confirm no policy value changed during formatting.
Validate the document after formatting if you plan to save.
The JSON document is easier to review and remains semantically unchanged.
Recovery: if formatting fails, fix JSON syntax first; trailing commas and missing braces are common causes.
Inspect imported unknown keys and raw-fallback values without losing them accidentally.
Open Review mode or a raw/unknown filtered list in All Settings.
Raw and unknown settings may come from import, schema differences, or values BPM cannot model visually.
Treat them as preservation and review items, not routine edits.
Filter or open Review items for raw, unknown, or imported settings.
Inspect the raw value, source, validation state, and schema channel.
Decide whether to preserve, remove, reset, or inspect the value in JSON Editor.
Save only after confirming the value should remain or be removed.
Raw and unknown values are preserved or removed intentionally.
Recovery: if the value might be important, export or compare the profile before removing it.
Use Configured mode to understand what the profile currently applies by domain, category, and source.
Open a saved profile in All Settings.
Configured mode focuses on values already present in the profile, not on every possible policy.
Domain summaries help you explain the active configuration.
Review the configured summary cards by domain or category.
Open a category to inspect the settings applied there.
Use source filters if you need to separate baseline, CIS, manual, imported, or raw values.
You can describe the active policy and managed preference values applied by the profile.
Recovery: if a value is missing, switch to Catalog mode or clear source filters before deciding it is absent.
Select a setting and inspect its value, source, validation, schema support, and product location.
Open All Settings and select a setting row from Review, Configured, Catalog, search, or a deep link.
The detail panel is the safe place to understand a single setting before editing it.
It shows value shape, source attribution, validation issues, and navigation context.
Select the setting row you need to understand.
Read the current value, source badge, validation messages, and schema/channel support.
Check the product location or related surface link if the setting is also covered elsewhere.
Decide whether to edit, remove, reset, or leave the value unchanged.
You understand what the setting does in this profile and what action is safe next.
Recovery: if the value shape is unclear, compare with JSON Editor or leave the setting unchanged until validation guidance is available.
Navigate All Settings categories and mapped control clusters to find related policy and preference controls.
Open All Settings in Configured or Catalog mode.
Categories group settings by product domain rather than by file location.
They help users move between browser access, privacy, search, extensions, raw/unmapped, and other clusters.
Open the category navigation or catalog summary.
Choose the domain or cluster that matches the configuration goal.
Review category counts for configured, attention, raw, or deprecated settings.
Open a setting detail or switch filters without losing the category context.
You can move through the settings inventory by product domain and reach the relevant detail panel.
Recovery: if a category does not contain the expected control, search by policy ID or inspect raw/unmapped items.
Remove a configured value or reset it back to the inherited baseline, preset, or unconfigured state.
Open the setting detail panel for a configured value.
Remove and reset actions are destructive for the selected value, so the user should understand source and downstream effects first.
Inspect the current value and source badge.
Choose Remove or Reset only for the setting you intend to change.
Read any warning or validation message shown by the detail panel.
Save the profile after confirming the value is absent, reset, or inherited as expected.
The setting no longer applies from the previous configured value.
Recovery: if the removal was unintended, reapply the previous value from history, import, comparison, or a saved source document.
Find CIS recommendations requiring manual review and decide whether to configure, document, or leave them for external verification.
Open All Settings Review mode for a profile that includes a CIS layer or CIS-derived source metadata.
Some CIS recommendations cannot be fully automated by BPM.
Review mode surfaces those items so the user can make an explicit decision without claiming certification.
Open Review mode and filter for CIS manual-review items if needed.
Read the recommendation identifiers, affected policy or preference, and current value.
Configure a supported value, document why manual verification remains, or leave the item intentionally unresolved.
Revalidate and record the decision before export or handoff.
CIS manual-review items are configured, documented, or intentionally left for external verification.
Recovery: if the recommendation cannot be mapped to a visible setting, keep the item in review and consult the CIS guide when that guide is authored.
Use Review mode to triage invalid, CIS manual-review, raw, unknown, deprecated, and imported items before routine editing.
Open a saved profile in All Settings.
Review mode is the default attention-first view.
It gathers settings that may require a decision before export, comparison, or handoff.
Open All Settings and stay in Review mode.
Read the review summary and grouped action cards.
Open each invalid, CIS manual-review, raw, unknown, deprecated, or imported item that applies to the profile.
Resolve the item, document why it remains, or move to the linked detail view for a deliberate edit.
Attention items are either resolved, intentionally retained, or ready for a focused detail edit.
Recovery: if Review looks empty but you expected issues, clear filters, refresh the profile, and confirm the selected schema channel.
Save a valid raw JSON document back to the canonical BPM profile.
The JSON document has been validated or the remaining warnings are understood.
Saving writes the raw document back through BPM normalization.
The saved profile can then be opened in Guided, All Settings, Compare, or export workflows.
Choose Save only when the top-level policies object and policy values are correct.
Wait for the saved status before leaving the route.
Reopen the profile or export policies.json when you need handoff evidence.
The BPM profile stores the JSON changes in the canonical profile model.
Recovery: if save fails, fix validation errors or return to a previous saved profile before editing again.
Search configured settings, available policies, known preferences, and setting actions from All Settings.
Search is shared across Review, Configured, and Catalog work.
It can lead to a setting, an action, or a filtered group.
Place focus in the All Settings search field.
Enter a policy ID, preference key, category, source, or plain-language term.
Choose a grouped result and confirm the target setting or action.
Clear the search when you return to browsing or filtering.
The matching setting or action is selected without losing the current profile context.
Recovery: if no result appears, confirm the schema channel and try a policy ID or preference key.
Trace a configured setting to baseline, CIS, manual, imported, or raw source attribution.
Open a configured setting in All Settings.
Source attribution helps explain why a value exists and whether changing it would override a baseline, CIS layer, manual edit, import, or raw fallback.
Open the setting detail or configured summary that shows source badges.
Identify whether the value comes from baseline, CIS, manual, imported, or raw source.
Follow related CIS or profile context links when a generated layer contributed the value.
Record the source before editing, removing, or resetting the setting.
You know where the configured value came from and can explain the impact of changing it.
Recovery: if source attribution is ambiguous, compare the profile with a clean baseline or inspect the imported source document.
Open All Settings for a saved profile when you need complete visual control beyond the shorter Guided workflow.
New unsaved drafts must be saved before All Settings can open.
All Settings is the complete visual editor for Firefox policies and known managed preferences.
It opens in Review mode so attention items are visible before broad catalog browsing.
Open the saved profile from the Library.
Choose the All Settings editor surface.
Confirm that Review, Configured, and Catalog modes are available.
Use the mode that matches the task: Review for attention, Configured for applied values, or Catalog for every supported setting.
The saved profile is open in All Settings with the correct mode available.
Recovery: if All Settings is unavailable, save the Guided draft first or reopen a saved profile from the Library.
Open the complete profile as a Firefox policies.json document for exact review or raw editing.
JSON Editor works on a saved profile and represents the profile as a Firefox boundary document.
JSON Editor is the raw document surface.
Use it when Guided or All Settings is too high-level for exact review, migration checks, troubleshooting, or raw values.
Open the saved profile from the Library or another editor.
Confirm the editor shows a top-level policies object and the download action is available.
Use JSON Editor only when exact raw document control is needed.
The current profile is visible as editable Firefox policies.json content.
Recovery: if the route cannot open, save the profile first or return to All Settings for visual editing.
Validate raw JSON syntax and Firefox policy values before saving.
Open JSON Editor with the document you want to check.
Validation distinguishes malformed JSON from policy or schema errors.
A document can parse as JSON and still fail policy validation.
If validation reports malformed JSON, fix syntax such as trailing commas or missing braces.
If validation reports policy errors, correct unsupported keys, wrong value types, or schema-channel mismatches.
Validate again until the status explains that the document is acceptable or the remaining issue is intentional for raw review.
The document has a known validation state before save or export.
Recovery: if errors are hard to read, use All Settings to inspect the affected policy or preference visually.
